articles.title: UP Politics: Election Heat Rises Over Caste, Religion and Vote Banks
articles.description: Ahead of the 2027 Uttar Pradesh Assembly election, political rhetoric has intensified, with the BJP and opposition parties exchanging allegations over caste, religion and voter blocs. At a BJP event in Meerut, Chief Minister Yogi Adityanath attacked his political opponents while invoking issues such as Lord Ram, the Kanwar Yatra and Sanatan traditions. BJP president Nitin Nabin also highlighted religious and cultural issues during his visit. The report links this messaging to the BJP’s focus on its Hindu voter base. The report cites CSDS-Lokniti data showing that in 2017, the BJP received around 47% of Hindu votes and 5% of Muslim votes, while the SP received 19% of Hindu votes and 46% of Muslim votes. In 2022, the BJP’s figures were 54% among Hindu voters and 8% among Muslim voters, while the SP received 26% and 79%, respectively. Meanwhile, AIMIM chief Asaduddin Owaisi is seeking an alliance in Uttar Pradesh and has set October 2 as a deadline for announcing his alliance plans. The Samajwadi Party has indicated that it intends to continue with its existing alliance arrangement. The report notes that AIMIM has not yet won a seat in the Uttar Pradesh Assembly. According to the cited voting-pattern data, the SP received 79% of Muslim votes in 2022, compared with 6% for the BSP, 3% for Congress and 8% for the BJP. The competing parties are therefore focusing heavily on Hindu and Muslim voter blocs as the 2027 election approaches.

articles.title: Dalit Battle: BJP, SP & BSP Step Up Outreach Ahead of 2027
articles.description: Uttar Pradesh’s political focus is increasingly turning toward the Dalit electorate ahead of the 2027 Assembly election. The report highlights the importance of Dalit voters and the efforts of the BJP, Samajwadi Party and BSP to strengthen their support among the community. The Samajwadi Party is promoting its PDA strategy, with the “D” representing Dalits, and has raised the issue of alleged attacks on statues of Dr B.R. Ambedkar. Akhilesh Yadav has also focused on reserved constituencies and has spoken about protecting the Constitution. In the 2024 Lok Sabha election, opposition parties won nine of Uttar Pradesh’s 17 SC-reserved seats, while the BJP won eight. The SP won seven, Congress one and Chandrashekhar Azad’s ASP(KR) one. The BJP, meanwhile, is seeking to maintain its support among Dalit voters through its outreach and welfare initiatives. Chief Minister Yogi Adityanath has also attacked previous SP governments over issues concerning Dalit icons and institutions. BSP chief Mayawati has separately sought to retain her party’s traditional Dalit support, accusing rival parties of turning to Dalit symbols only during elections. The 2024 Lok Sabha results also saw the BSP win no seat in Uttar Pradesh, while the SP won 37 and BJP 33 overall. Overall, the report focuses on how the BJP, SP and BSP are positioning themselves around Dalit representation, Ambedkar’s legacy and reserved constituencies ahead of the 2027 Uttar Pradesh Assembly election.

articles.title: Jamui Horror: 3 Arrested Over Viral Harassment Video; Political War Erupts in Bihar
articles.description: In Bihar’s Jamui, police have taken major action in the case involving a viral video showing alleged harassment and molestation of a minor girl and her friend. ADG Law and Order S. Anupam said that three accused have been arrested so far, while the identities of seven to eight youths have emerged and their roles are being investigated. A case has been registered under the POCSO Act and other sections, and an SIT has been formed. Police are also checking the accused’s criminal records. Action is also being taken against those spreading the viral video. So far, 32 social media accounts—13 Facebook, 12 Instagram and 7 X accounts—have faced action. The incident has also triggered a political dispute in Bihar. JD(U) state president Umesh Singh Kushwaha called it an isolated incident and said the government is sensitive and taking action. RJD leader Tejashwi Yadav, however, accused the government of failing to ensure women’s safety and alleged that the administration tries to suppress such cases.

articles.title: UNGA 2026: World Leaders Attend 'Partners For Multilateralism Summit' In New York
articles.description: World leaders gathered in New York City on September 21 for the Partners for Multilateralism Summit, held on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly. The summit was co-hosted by European Council President António Costa, along with Kenya, Australia, Barbados, Canada, Brazil, and India. The meeting focused on strengthening multilateral cooperation and supporting international institutions, particularly the United Nations. In his opening remarks, Costa highlighted the importance of collective action and cooperation among countries to address shared global challenges. He stated that the summit’s core objective was to support the work of the UN and other multilateral frameworks while ensuring that international commitments lead to practical outcomes. The participation of leaders from different regions reflected a broad effort to promote cooperation and coordinated action. Overall, the summit emphasized the importance of multilateralism, shared responsibility, and translating diplomatic commitments into concrete measures that can address global issues effectively.

articles.title: Trump-Mamdani NYC Meeting; President Defends Media Restrictions, Housing Plans In Focus
articles.description: Trump and New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani held a joint news conference on September 21 after meeting at Gracie Mansion, focusing on areas where the two could cooperate, particularly housing affordability and New York City’s high cost of living. Mamdani said they discussed expanding housing development, including the potential redevelopment of Sunnyside Yard in Queens. The proposed project could create approximately 12,000 homes and 30,000 jobs. Trump said the development should include a substantial share of housing for low- and moderate-income residents, while pointing to his previous experience with such projects. The discussion also touched on broader affordability challenges facing New Yorkers. During the press conference, Trump renewed his criticism of several news organizations, calling them “fake news” and defending restrictions on access for some outlets at the White House. Trump argued that news organizations have an obligation to report fairly and defended his decision to restrict access to outlets he accused of publishing inaccurate or fictional reports.

articles.title: ‘FAKE NEWS has grown like cancer’: Trump vs Media erupts as CNN, MSNOW & Politico sue White House
articles.description: The Trump administration’s latest clash with the media has escalated dramatically - with three major news organizations suing the White House, while the television networks covering the president have now suspended pooled coverage of his events. CNN, MS NOW and Politico filed a joint lawsuit against the Trump administration on September 21, days after their reporters were barred from the White House. The three outlets say the administration revoked their journalists’ credentials because Trump objected to the content of their reporting. They are calling the move an illegal action and “a blatant violation” of the First Amendment. The reporters’ White House access was cut off over the weekend. CNN’s Betsy Klein, MS NOW’s Akayla Gardner and Politico’s Cheyenne Haslett were among those denied entry, with their press credentials disabled or confiscated. The White House had said the outlets were being barred because of what Trump described as “fake news.” But the news organizations argue that the government cannot selectively exclude journalists simply because the president dislikes their coverage.

articles.title: Re: Assisted dying bill rejected: how doctors helped shape the debate
articles.description: Agreement: I Agree Body: Dear Editor, Re: Assisted dying bill rejected: how doctors helped shape the debate by Adrian O’Dowd BMJ 2026;394:e100854 http://doi.org/10.1136/bmj-2026-100854 Published: 14 September 2026 I read with interest O’Dowd’s recent news review of the rejection of the Terminally Ill Adults (End of Life) Bill. As an NHS nurse working in ITU who has had a personal family experience of assisted dying, I am both personally and professionally devastated that legislation has not been passed. My devastation is compounded by the fact that MPs had previously demonstrated majority support for this legislation, with polling demonstrating overwhelming majority public support as well – support MPs were unable to coalesce. This has been, and will be remembered as, a failure of parliamentary process and a failure of government to do the right thing. Though palliative medicine is brilliant, in our work we routinely see patients suffering at the end of life despite exemplary palliative care. It is misleading to argue that palliative care is a panacea. There have been missed opportunities by the BMA and others to challenge such significant misleading arguments by practicing physicians during these debates. Conservative MP Rebecca Smith quoted palliative care consultants in her constituency who said they were ‘not prepared to take part in assisted dying’, remarking that they would ‘leave the profession’ over the issue. This is hyperbole at best and patient abandonment at worst. It was clear in this legislation (and in legislation across the globe) that clinicians are not mandated to participate in assisted dying, with conscientious objectors consistently respected. Smith asks ‘How can we offer palliative care at the same time as assisted dying?’ – I will tell you how, through the personal experience of my Mum, who resided in Canada prior to her death. Diagnosed with metastatic melanoma, she received palliative radiotherapy and met with various oncologists and palliative care consultants who deemed she was not fit for immunotherapy nor any other therapies. She chose to have an assisted death at home, having been assessed for it by both hospital and community doctors who were entirely separate from her palliative care team. In the end, her death was facilitated by a GP, not by anyone involved in her palliative care, though as a family we would have been more than happy either way. Whether or not her palliative care team were personally supportive of her decision or were conscientious objectors was never elucidated to us, and was entirely irrelevant. In your article Labour MP Zubir Ahmed expressed concerns about assisted dying with respect to defining terminal illness, mentioning predicting individual patient responses to immunotherapy as a concrete example of where this can be difficult. Though I would concede this point, I would argue the answer to this isn’t to then block choice from those facing death, but to instead widen the criteria to those with unendurable suffering as defined by the patient. Prognostication of less than six months to live is entirely arbitrary and unnecessary - and in my Mum’s case, had she been a candidate for immunotherapy, I’m confident she would have initiated that treatment whilst simultaneously exploring her other options, one of which was assisted dying. In a misguided attempt to ‘protect’ patients and ensure equity, MPs have failed to pass safe legislation and have chosen to continue a true inequity, whereby wealthy UK residents can travel to Europe to seek an assisted death, and those without the means to do so are left adrift. I am so grateful my Mum emigrated to Canada and had the choice as she faced death, and I only wish the same could be true for all of us residents in the UK today. Sincerely, Luke Costello, RN Board Member of My Death, My Decision No competing Interests: No competing interests The following competing Interests: Board member of My Death, My Decision.
